Kandel’s work with the sea slug was so profound because the mechanisms of memory are evolutionarily conserved. The same basic rules that govern learning in a sea slug apply in more complex creatures, including us. Chemical signaling. Synaptic plasticity. Patterned responses driven by stimulus and repetition. This helped lay the groundwork for modern memory research and continues to inform our understanding of human learning, behavior, and cognitive therapy. We have looked inside our own brains and across the spectrum of biological life to study and learn from less intelligent creatures, but now we are doing something wholly different. We have created a learning engine that is beyond biology, plugged into the power grid, and on a path to far exceed our own intelligence. And we sort of know how it works. Back to DeepMind’s AlphaGo artificial intelligence engine defeating Lee Sedol in 2016. 4 Go is a game of intuition and flow. Masters don’t calculate every possibility—they feel their way through the board. The number of legal board configurations exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. For years, it was believed no machine could match the subtlety of human play. But AlphaGo didn’t just win; it surprised the experts. It made moves that human professional players had never considered—moves that at first seemed bizarre but later were recognized as brilliant. But here’s the important bit: We didn’t teach AlphaGo how to play Go. We didn’t tell it any moves or give it any strategy. We simply gave it the rules and let it play millions of games against itself. We taught it to learn—and it did. Then it made moves we had never imagined. Let’s take that principle forward from AlphaGo to the more modern AI moving so fast into our world. On October 8, 2023, Scott Pelley, on the TV show 60 Minutes , was interviewing a man named Geoffrey Hinton, who is often called the godfather of AI. Scott Pelley asked, incredulously, “What do you mean we don’t know exactly how it works? It was designed by people.” 5 Hinton immediately interrupted him: “No, it wasn’t. What we did was we designed the learning algorithm. That’s a bit like designing the principle of evolution. But when this learning algorithm then interacts with data, it produces complicated neural networks that are good at doing things. But we don’t really understand exactly how they do those things.” 6 For context, Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded jointly with John J. Hopfield, for “foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks,” and he was the vice president and engineering fellow at Google from 2013 to 2023. 7 It is a really crucial distinction he makes—the difference between programming a computer to do something versus programming a computer to learn . The AI built its own complex neural connections, its own model of the world. And that is exactly why modern AI is both so powerful and so mysterious to its own creators. Now, there are people who will say that we do generally know how AI works, and they are partly right. But as you will come to see, the people building it occasionally set up controlled experiments to see how it will behave and are often surprised by its behavior, including acting in its own best interest when under threat. I can tell you that it took dynamic software and hardware infrastructure, including the integration of three different AI models working together, at Amplifire, the learning company that I run, to ensure that it stayed on task and performed as expected. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves. Major AI advancements flow directly from our advancing understanding of how the human brain learns. We will explore how our brain’s energy constraints ironically drove the evolution of human intelligence and how decoding that process gave us the blueprint for machine learning. But unlike our brains, AI is plugged into the power grid. You see, for most of human history, advanced intelligence has meant one thing: us! We have looked not only inside our own brains, but also across the spectrum of biological life to study the many lesser versions of intelligence, and that search has helped us decode our own. In Some Ways It Began with Jane Goodall and the Chimps In 2025, when we lost Jane Goodall, we lost one of the most amazing humans to ever live. One of the insane benefits of being a moderately successful entrepreneur is that you get the opportunity to meet and support people whom you might never encounter otherwise. Meeting Jane was one of those moments for me. I hosted a fundraising dinner for the Jane Goodall Institute at my house in Boulder, Colorado. When Jane arrived at my house that morning, I was mesmerized by her gentle presence. She set up camp in my guesthouse. For lunch, we walked along Boulder Creek, and about every twenty-five feet or so, someone walking in the other direction would stop in their tracks when they saw her. Some would say hi, and others would just look in shock. But she always made eye contact and smiled regardless. After about ten minutes of this, I told her that I was extremely introverted and asked her if the constant recognition was challenging. Her response surprised me. She said that she was happiest alone in the forest with the chimps but that the world was in trouble, and she had her part to play. She said that there was the public Jane Goodall and the private Jane, and that she never forgot the difference. By some amazing twist of fate, Jane was finishing up writing her New York Times best-selling book, Seeds of Hope , and she decided to stay in Boulder for five days to finish it up.
